analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans and public programs to cover HIV prevention drugs with no patient cost-sharing.
analysis.headline: The bill got no committee vote, no floor action, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, after being referred to the Senate health committee with 1 cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require private insurance, employer plans, Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, the VA, TRICARE, and the Indian Health Service to cover FDA-approved drugs that prevent HIV — plus lab work and follow-up visits — at zero cost to the patient, with no pre-authorization hoops. It would bar life, disability, and long-term care insurers from denying coverage or raising premiums because someone takes HIV prevention medication. It would also fund programs so uninsured people can get the drugs and direct a CDC public awareness campaign.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 1.2 million Americans who could benefit from PrEP — especially gay and bisexual men, transgender women, and Black and Latino communities, where usage is lowest (only 11% of eligible Black Americans and 12% of eligible women were prescribed it in 2022, versus 82% of eligible White people). Uninsured and underinsured people would gain access through new federal grants, and anyone taking PrEP could no longer be penalized by life or disability insurers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of HIV, especially Black and Latino communities

how_it_helps.text: Adds HIV prevention drugs, lab tests, and clinical follow-up to the list of preventive services private plans must cover without any cost-sharing, and bans pre-authorization for them except when a therapeutically equivalent drug is covered without restrictions.

Extends no-cost HIV prevention coverage to Medicare (both Part B services and Part D drugs), Medicaid, CHIP, the Federal Employees Health Benefits program, the VA, TRICARE, and the Indian Health Service, with most provisions effective for plan years starting January 1, 2025.
Makes it unlawful for life, disability, or long-term care insurers to deny coverage, refuse to issue a policy, or raise premiums because a person takes HIV prevention medication.

Directs HHS to award grants to states, tribes, and clinics to get PrEP and post-exposure prophylaxis to uninsured and underinsured people, and requires a CDC public education campaign focused on communities where use is lowest.

Gives patients a private right of action with attorney fees if insurers violate the coverage rules, and requires HHS, Labor, and Treasury to police compliance with annual insurer data submissions and reports to Congress.
Directs HHS to update privacy rules so someone on a family plan can use these benefits without the policyholder finding out.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers bear the cost of free coverage and compliance reporting, which flows into premiums for enrollees generally. Taxpayers fund the expanded Medicaid, Medicare, VA, and IHS coverage and the grant program. Life, disability, and long-term care insurers would spread the banned rating practice across their remaining policyholders. Brand-name HIV drug makers gain a guaranteed, funded market at negotiated prices the bill does not touch.

drawbacks.text: Requiring plans to cover PrEP and all related services at no cost adds to insurer costs, which are typically passed into premiums paid by all enrollees.

The ban on rating or denying life, disability, and long-term care coverage for PrEP users blocks insurers from pricing what they view as actuarial risk, which would spread costs across other policyholders — a standard objection to any anti-discrimination insurance mandate.
The private right of action with mandatory attorney fees could generate litigation against insurers over coverage disputes.
The grant and awareness programs are authorized at unspecified sums and would need annual appropriations from Congress.
States could delay Medicaid and CHIP compliance if state legislation is needed, so coverage would not arrive everywhere on the same date.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and well documented in the bill's own findings: PrEP cuts the risk of HIV from sex by more than 99%, yet only about a third of the people who could benefit filled prescriptions in 2022, with stark racial gaps. Cost is modest relative to the alternative — each prevented HIV infection avoids a lifetime of treatment the public eventually pays for through Medicaid and federal programs. The main honest costs are higher premiums for insured people broadly and forgone risk-pricing for life and disability insurers. This is a targeted, evidence-based mandate rather than a sweeping entitlement, but it is a real mandate, and its costs do not disappear; they are redistributed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in June 2023, and the committee never took it up; no vote ever happened in either chamber before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Tina Smith introduced the bill on June 22, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That referral was the bill's only action: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote is recorded in its entire history.
It drew a single cosponsor, one of 48 Senate Democrats, and no Senate Republican signed on.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers avoid the new no-cost coverage mandate, compliance reporting, and lawsuits, and life, disability, and long-term care insurers keep the ability to rate or decline applicants who take HIV prevention drugs. Meanwhile the gap the bill targeted persists: about two-thirds of the people who could benefit from PrEP still do not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers; the PrEP access gap persists

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PrEP Access and Coverage Act of 2023 and became its only Senate sponsor.

for.name: 1 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senators joined.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in June 2023 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; the only recorded support was two Democrats (Smith and one cosponsor), and no Republican is recorded as either supporting or opposing the bill.

industries.note: Plans would have to cover HIV prevention drugs, labs, and follow-up with zero patient cost-sharing, no pre-authorization, annual compliance data submissions, and exposure to lawsuits with attorney fees. Because the bill removes insurers' ability to shift these costs to patients, insurers' savings come directly at the expense of the people the bill protects.

industries.industry: Life, disability, and long-term care insurers
industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to deny coverage, refuse a policy, or raise premiums because someone takes HIV prevention medication, eliminating a rating and underwriting practice these insurers currently use.

Mandatory coverage across every major insurance program plus federal grants for the uninsured would guarantee payment for PrEP drugs at prices the bill does not regulate, expanding the manufacturers' market. Wider access helps patients, but the public pays list prices with no negotiating lever in the bill.
